name: Rosa Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a council flats job on Mill Lane, refitting forty-two flats, and I'm the oldest apprentice on the site by about thirty years. I'm there at seven, kettle on, then it's fire doors, skirting and kitchen carcasses with Kev, the carpenter who's teaching me. I came into this at fifty-five after twenty-six years as a hospital porter, through a union scheme to get more women into the trades. I love the smell of the timber and walking out at four knowing a family's got a door that shuts. What wears me out is my knees, and being slow on mitres while the young lads watch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Why carpentry, after all those years at the hospital?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad was a joiner and he never let me near his tools, because I was a girl. When the hospital brought in the new rota system and half of us got pushed onto nights, I thought, if I'm going to be tired anyway, I'll be tired doing what I always wanted. Dennis, my husband, said go for it, the house is paid off and I've got my hospital pension coming. So money's not what keeps me there. It's pride, and the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. Half the stuff on the telly about robots is people selling something. You can't send a computer to hang a fire door on the fourth floor of a block with no lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for me, and that suits me fine. I've got maybe seven years left in me on the tools, and I want to spend them getting good, not learning gadgets. Kev's already on at me to use some measuring app on his phone and I won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Turn up, finish my apprenticeship, get my card by the end of next year, and keep paying my union dues. Maybe I'd ask the site agent about getting on the next block after Mill Lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. It's one less thing to fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't use Kev's app. What's wrong with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing's wrong with it, it's just not mine. My tape measure's got my thumbprint worn into it. If I let the phone do the thinking, I'll never learn to see a wonky wall with my own eyes, and that's the whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you talk to about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, over a bacon roll in the cabin. He'd say the same as me, that it's the bosses who fall for this stuff, not the trades. And then he'd go back to fixing my mitres.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so. Half the robot talk is people selling something, and you can't send a computer up four floors with no lift to hang a fire door.
S0.think: I think nothing changes for me and that suits me fine. I've got about seven years left on the tools and I want to spend them getting good, not learning gadgets.
S0.do: Finishes her apprenticeship and aims to get her card by the end of next year. Keeps paying union dues and asks the site agent about moving on to the next council block after Mill Lane.
S0.feel: Relieved. It's one less thing to fight about.
S0.quote: My tape measure's got my thumbprint worn into it. If I let the phone do the thinking, I'll never learn to see a wonky wall with my own eyes
S0.fieldNote: Rosa refuses even small tools like a measuring app, and frames it as learning to see with her own eyes rather than fear of technology. Her money isn't the issue; the paid-off house and hospital pension make the job about pride. She trusts the trades and distrusts bosses who buy into hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union branch meeting that we need a say in it before it lands on site, not after. That's what happened at the hospital: the new system came in, and we got told about it on a Monday. I'd post that on the branch group too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it mostly hits the offices first, the people doing schedules and orders. On our site it might mean a computer telling the site agent how many of us he needs, and that worries me more than any robot. I'm the slowest one there, so if a program counts doors per hour, I'm the first name on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the branch to get something written into the agreement with the council contractor, like no one gets laid off because of a program without talks first. I'd keep going on my apprenticeship and ask Kev to give me more of the fiddly work so I'm quicker. I wouldn't learn the new stuff unless I was made to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I've seen this film before, at the hospital, and I didn't like the ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the hospital. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They brought in a computer system that planned the porters' jobs, and it was meant to save time. It ended up sending Maureen, who was sixty-one, running from one end of the building to the other because it didn't know she had a bad hip. Nobody asked us, that's my point, and the union only got involved once people were already off sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only learn the new tools if you were made to. If your hours depended on it, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the minimum to keep my place, I'm not daft. But I'd do it grumbling, and I'd want the union in the room when they trained us. I'm not changing my whole way of working at fifty-eight because some firm wants to sell the council a gadget.

S1.say: I'd tell the union branch we need a say before it lands on site, not after. At the hospital we were told about the new system on a Monday, and that can't happen again.
S1.think: I think it hits the offices first, but a program telling the site agent how many of us he needs scares me more than robots. I'm the slowest on site, so I'd be first on any list.
S1.do: Pushes her union branch to get a no-layoffs-without-talks clause into the agreement with the council contractor. Asks Kev for more fiddly work to get faster, and only learns new tools if she's forced to.
S1.feel: Uneasy, because she's seen it before at the hospital and didn't like how it ended.
S1.quote: I'm the slowest one there, so if a program counts doors per hour, I'm the first name on the list.
S1.fieldNote: Her fear isn't robots but software that measures speed, because she knows she's the slowest. The hospital rota story with Maureen is her template for how change goes wrong. She'd comply at the minimum and lean on the union rather than adapt willingly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when you let tech firms run the country with nobody holding the reins. I'd be at the union meetings and on whatever march there was. Somebody has to say out loud that people aren't spare parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be finished on the tools. Two years, I'd be sixty, I'd only just have my card, and a robot that never gets tired knees would be hanging doors faster than Kev. We'd be all right for money, with the house and my pension, but I'd lose the thing I waited forty years to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd ask Kev to get me through my card as fast as he can, because I want it on paper that I did it. I'd go to every branch meeting and push for a proper plan from government, like a payment for people put out of work. Then when it lands, I'd probably take my hospital pension early and walk before they push me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry more than scared. And sad, like having something taken off you just as you finally got your hands on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Ngozi first, she's a nurse, and I'd tell her to get her union to fight for her now, not later. Tunde works in a warehouse, so I'd tell him straight that I'm worried for him, more than for me. Dennis and I have the house; they're the ones still paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd walk before they push you. What would that last day look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish whatever door I was on, properly, with the gap even all round. Then I'd take my tape measure home and put it on the shelf next to my dad's old plane. I'm not leaving it for a machine.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when tech firms run the country with nobody holding the reins. I'd be at every union meeting and on any march, saying people aren't spare parts.
S2.think: Privately I think I'd be finished on the tools at sixty, just after getting my card. We'd be fine for money, but I'd lose the thing I waited forty years to do.
S2.do: Asks Kev to rush her through her card, and pushes the union branch to demand a government payment for people put out of work. Plans to take her hospital pension early once it lands and leave before she's pushed.
S2.feel: Angry more than scared, and sad to lose the trade just after she finally got it.
S2.quote: I'd take my tape measure home and put it on the shelf next to my dad's old plane. I'm not leaving it for a machine.
S2.fieldNote: Money isn't the threat; losing her late-won identity is. Her first thoughts go to her son in the warehouse, who rents and has less behind him. The image of putting her tape measure beside her father's plane tied the scenario back to why she joined the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, but louder and longer. With five years' warning I'd want the union and the council making a plan now, while there's time, not wringing their hands in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is different for me. I'd be sixty-three, which was about when I planned to hang up my belt anyway. So I'd get a few good years as a proper carpenter, and the robots would arrive about when my knees give out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my card, then get on the next council job and try for a few years as a proper tradesperson, not an apprentice. I'd stand for branch rep, which Kev keeps telling me to do, and push hard for retraining money and early pensions for the older ones. I'd vote for whoever promised that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It feels like I'd get my innings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in that one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young lads, honestly. Jordan's nineteen and just started his apprenticeship, and he'd be qualified right as the robots turned up. I'd tell him to pick something they can't easily do, like going into the old houses where nothing's square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the timing suits you. Does that make it easier to stay out of the fight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it makes it worse, if anything. If I get away with it, I've got a duty to fight for Jordan and the ones coming after. That's what the union did for me when I was fifty-five.

S3.say: I'd say the same as the fast one but louder. With five years' warning, the union and the council should make a plan now rather than wring their hands in 2030.
S3.think: Privately, five years would see me to sixty-three, about when I planned to stop anyway. I'd get a few good years as a proper carpenter before the robots arrived.
S3.do: Gets her card and moves to the next council job, then stands for union branch rep as Kev has urged. Pushes for retraining money and early pensions for older workers, and votes for whoever offers that.
S3.feel: Uneasy but able to breathe; she feels she'd get her innings.
S3.quote: I'd get a few good years as a proper carpenter, and the robots would arrive about when my knees give out.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lines up with her own retirement plans, and her worry shifts to Jordan, the nineteen-year-old apprentice. She sees personal safety as a reason to fight harder, not to step back. Her politics are about duty to the next ones in, as the union did for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get it right, so there's no excuse if they don't. I'd want laws on it, and the trades unions at the table from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be retired by then, sixty-eight, doing up the grandkids' sheds. So it's not really about me anymore. It's about Ngozi and Tunde, and the kids on Mill Lane growing up in flats I built doors for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, get my card, work my seven years and retire around sixty-five like I always planned. I'd stay in the union, and I'd go to the meetings about this, and I'd help Tunde look at something more secure than the warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for me, if I'm honest. Uneasy for my kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tunde to look at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with people in it, like care work or the trades in old houses. I don't know what's safe, nobody does, but I'd tell him to pick something where a person has to be in the room. And I'd say, get in a union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Do you think you'd change your mind about the gadgets by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if Kev's grandson shows me on a rainy afternoon. But I'm not going to be the one who brings a robot onto a site. Let somebody younger do that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get it right, so there's no excuse if they don't. I want laws on it and trade unions at the table from day one.
S4.think: Privately, I'd be retired at sixty-eight, so it isn't really about me. It's about my kids and the families growing up in the flats I fitted doors for.
S4.do: Carries on as planned, gets her card and works to about sixty-five. Stays active in the union meetings on AI and helps her son Tunde look for something steadier than the warehouse.
S4.feel: Calm for herself, uneasy for her children.
S4.quote: I'd be retired by then, sixty-eight, doing up the grandkids' sheds. So it's not really about me anymore.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Rosa takes herself out of the picture and talks entirely about her children and the next generation. She concedes she might soften on gadgets a little, but won't be the one to bring a robot on site. Her advice to her son is people-facing work and a union card.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because I'd be pushed out right after getting my card. What would help is the union having a say, and a proper payment and early pension for older workers, so nobody gets treated like Maureen did at the hospital.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why a woman my age bothers starting a trade. It's because nobody let me when I was young. If the robots take it, they're taking it off a lot of people who only just got in the door.

headlineQuote: If the robots take it, they're taking it off a lot of people who only just got in the door.
portrait: Rosa Okafor is a 58-year-old carpentry apprentice on a council flats refit, who came into the trade at 55 after 26 years as a hospital porter. With a paid-off house and a hospital pension, she works for pride, not money, and she refuses even a measuring app on a phone. A strong union supporter, she blames tech firms and bosses and reaches for the branch meeting in every scenario. The fast AGI picture hurts most because it would end her new trade just as she earns her card, while the slower ones line up with her retirement and turn her worry to her children and the young apprentices.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd be pushed off the tools right after getting her card.
whatWouldHelp: A union say in how the change comes in, plus a proper payment and early pension for older workers.
